Bitcoin

By: James Carroll | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The best performing currency in 2015 was not the dollar - it wasn't a currency at all.

Summary:
Bitcoin, a digital and decentralized cryptocurrency, staged a late comeback in 2015 to overtake the dollar by a whopping 35% by the end of the year. Major banking institutions all over the world are signing onto the underlying technology - the blockchain - which is a database that is hardened against tampering and revision. However there are still some challenges facing Bitcoin and it has been a tumuilous journey for the technology recently after a key developer, Mike Hearn, stated that he was no longer confident in the commodity. 2016 will be the year that Bitcoin is forced to grow up.

Bitcoin in South Africa is legal and falls under the Financial Intelligence Centre Act 38 of 2001. There are currently 2 exchanges in South Africa - BitX and Icex. BitX received a $4m funding injection from Naspers in July 2015. With a combination of graphics and experts we would describe what Bitcoin is and pose the question of is it worth buying it to try and preserve a rapidly declining rand. I am still trying to lock down a (major) success or failure subject but it's still very new for South Africans. Failing that - maybe an amateur day-trader that isn't me?

Press Release:


Bitcoin
Is a digital decentralised currency such as Bitcoin worth investing in? Major financial institutions the world over paying attention to the online crytocurrency that has enabled millions of online transactions since its creation. Carte Blanche asks: What is behind the Bitcoin empire?


Script:


Bitcoin
23 April 2016
James Carroll


CLAIRE ON-CAM
A defining aspect of civilization was the creation of currency, whether it be shells, spices, gold or paper. Money is such an integral part of society but it’s true nature remains a mystery.

CLAIRE VO
As the rand continues its slow path of recovery, more people are transacting in a commodity of the future : Bitcoin.

The premise of Bitcoin can be tricky to explain – Bitcoin is a crypto-currency, virtual, that exists digitally. While governments make more money by printing it at the mint, Bitcoins are extracted from cyberspace the way gold is extracted from the earth.
It has no central authority, there’s no delay in sending money and the transaction fees cost cents.

It’s an open-source technology that has that sprouted hundreds of clones and is forcing financial institutions to re-examine their methodologies.

CLAIRE ON-CAM
Technology has been hailed as the great leveler. Could Bitcoin level the playing fields even further?

IAN MERRINGTON
Technology is a leveler because it takes out the role of the middleman and it takes out the role of government and it takes out the role of big corporations because it empowers people.

CLAIRE VO
Ian Merrington is CEO of The Cape Innovation and Technology Initiative.

IAN MERRINGTON
Now as the internet moves into an internet of value with potential currency, Bitcoin being a great example, what stops people trading from a phone to phone, person to person, what’s commonly known as peer to peer, again it removes the need for a bank. So again technology is very empowering and very enabling and obviously very transformative.

CLAIRE VO
Probably because it works outside of government regulation and subverts the traditional banking system, Bitcoin has been outlawed in some countries around the world and heavily frowned upon by others.

Virtual currencies are currently unregulated in South Africa. In a joint statement issued by the Financial Intelligence Centre, National Treasury, the South African Reserve Bank and the South African Revenue Service, they urged caution, due to the high degree of anonymity and that transactions are irreversible.




CLAIRE ON-CAM
The concept of Bitcoin was first published in 2008 by an unknown person using the pseudonym Satorshi Nakamoto and the first Bitcoin software was released the following year.

CLAIRE VO
After the release of the software, he participated with others on the project via mailing lists, until he finally began to fade from the community toward the end of 2010.

Nakamoto worked with people on the open-source team, but took care never to reveal anything personal about himself, and the last anyone heard from him was in the spring of 2011, when he said that he had “moved on to other things”.

But where do Bitcoins come from?

Locally, Bitcoins can be bought for money through exchanges as it’s treated as a commodity rather than a straightforward currency. One of these exchanges is BitX, based in Cape Town.

Carel van Wyk is one of the founders of the company.

CLAIRE ON-CAM
What does BitX do?

CAREL VAN WYK
Our core focus is making it safe and simple for the individual to store the Bitcoin, to send the Bitcoin, to spend the Bitcoin as well as convert the Bitcoin to local currency and back.

CLAIRE ON-CAM
Carel, could you explain to me, what’s the difference between a Bitcoin transaction and a credit card or electronic transaction?

CAREL VAN WYK
Bitcoin transactions are faster and cheaper, but specifically as a customer its safer because you don’t have to provide your credit card or any personal information, and as a merchant there’s also no fraud risk if you accept a payment with at least one confirmation. And, as well as access to a wide audience of people, you can accept payment from anywhere in the world as a Bitcoin wallet.

CLAIRE VO
Exchanges are made through wallet software rather than the traditional wallet in your back pocket. Like a commodity the monetary value of your Bitcoin is set entirely by the supply and demand of the market.

With no thing to hold in your hand, Bitcoin’s value might seem indecipherable and as a newer concept it does tend to fluctuate. It surged in November 2013 when the value topped $1200 and was briefly worth more than an ounce of gold. It then tumbled to 20% of its value and on November 1st 2015, a single Bitcoin was worth $325 and as of April the value topped $450.

And again like gold, the number of Bitcoin is finite, capped at 21 million. The production rate is scheduled to halve every 4 years to ensure that a value of a Bitcoin is not lost. At the current rate of production tzzhis means that supply will run out in 2140.

As it stands today, over a century before the deadline, roughly 64% of Bitcoin remain unused in their respective accounts appreciating and depreciating with time.

DEMO

CLAIRE VO
Currently there are over 100,000 merchants worldwide that accept Bitcoin – everything from groceries to airtime and beyond. Perhaps the most high profile of accepter of the currency is Virgin Galactic – pay for your futuristic journey with futuristic money.

Bitcoin and cryptocurrencies are also more than just virtual money – the monetary aspect is just the tip of the iceberg. The real power lies in the open public ledger that is distributed across the network that is transparent. It’s called the blockchain. In the blockchain, all transactions are logged, including the time, date, participants and amount of every single transaction. Each nodes in the network owns a full of copy of the blockchain. On the basis of complicated mathematical principals the transactions are verified by the so-called bitcoin miners who maintain the ledger. The mathematical principals also ensure that these nodes automatically and continuously agree about the current state of the ledger and every transaction in it. If anyone tries to corrupt a transaction, the nodes will not arrive at a consensus and will refuse to incorporate the transaction in the blockchain so every transaction is public. It’s almost as though there is a notary present for every transaction.

IAN MERRINGTON
I think we’ve seen a lot of businesses being disrupted lately through innovation. The travel industry comes to mind, when last did you use your travel agent to book a flight? We’ve seen what’s been happening with Air BnB, we’ve seen what’s happening with Uber. And effectively, digital currency and crypto-currency such as Bitcoin really is just innovation using a tech platform

CLAIRE VO
The ledger doesn’t care if the bitcoin represents a certain amount of euros or dollars, or anything else of value or property for that matter. Users can decide for themselves what a unit of bitcoin represents.

Bitcoin is divisable in a 100,000,000 units and each unit is individually identifiable and programmable. This means users can assign properties to each unit. Users can program a unit to represent a eurocent, or a share in a company, a kilowatt-hour of energy or a digital certificate of ownership. Because of this Bitcoin is much more than simply money and payments. A Bitcoin can represent many kinds of property.

CLAIRE ON-CAM:
Most people would associate Bitcoin with illegal activities and anonymous exchanges but that isn’t the case.

CLAIRE VO
Jonathan Levin is a co-founder at Chainalysis, a company that looks at what exchanges are happening on the blockchain.

JONATHAN LEVIN
The interesting thing about Bitcoin compared to traditional financial systems is that you have one financial ledger. So every transaction is recorded in the same ledger and each one of those participants, so the Bitcoin businesses, the banks and the government regulators, all have access to the same transactional information. And when that happens everyone can be proactive in investigations. Its no longer the case that only the Bitcoin business can report suspicious activity to the regulator, now the regulator can also ask questions to the Bitcoin business, like “listen I saw this transaction looked a little bit high, why wasn’t it reported?’

CLAIRE ON-CAM
Does your service also provide legitimacy to crypto-currency?

JONATHAN LEVIN
Yes, because if you think about in the traditional banking context there’s a lot of emphasis put on preventing money laundering, knowing your customer well and essentially assessing the risk of every customer that you do business with. And in the Bitcoin circle, what happened originally was, people couldn’t know what type of activity their customers were doing with their Bitcoins. And then what we do is we actually analyze all the bad activity, so I find out the cyber crime and drug trafficking and stuff like that, that Bitcoin gets used for. And I can alert services about whether they’re about to do business with those types of activity and they can then report it in the same way that they do in the traditional financial world.

CLAIRE ON-CAM
I know earlier on we were talking about banks, how receptive have they been to this new block chain and crypto-currency?

CAREL VAN WYK
In general, when it comes to technology, banks move quite slowly, but we think they will get there in the end and I don’t think there’s a big bank at the moment that doesn’t have a team working on block chain and investigating it and understanding what its about. So I do think the banks are doing the responsible thing to at least understand the technology.

CLAIRE ON-CAM
Whether you understand it or not, the face of money has forever been changed. Could this be a case of adapt or die?

CAREL VAN WYK
I think just take note of the growing momentum behind it and it might be good for everybody to have a little bit of Bitcoin to say “I’m a part of this”.

END.




PROMOS
10s
As the rand continues its path of recovery, more people are transacting in a commodity of the internet : Bitcoin
I think just take note of the growing momentum behind it and it might be good for everybody to have a little bit of Bitcoin to say “I’m a part of this”.


15s
Is a digital decentralised currency such as Bitcoin worth investing in? Major financial institutions are paying attention to the online crytocurrency that has enabled millions of transactions since its creation. What is behind the Bitcoin empire?

15s

It’s an open-source technology that has that sprouted hundreds of clones and is forcing banks to re-examine their methodologies. What is Bitcoin?
